blocks.h2: What Does an Ejector Pump Do?
blocks.body: An ejector pump moves wastewater from fixtures below the main sewer line, like a basement bathroom or laundry room, up to the level where gravity can carry it to the sewer. It sits in a sealed basin, usually in the basement floor. When the wastewater reaches a set level, a float triggers the pump and it pushes everything up and out. It's often confused with a [sump pump](/highland-park/sump-pumps), which removes groundwater, not wastewater.

img.alt: J. Blanton plumber working on the discharge pipe of a basement sump pump

blocks.h2: Signs Your Ejector Pump Is Failing
blocks.intro: Ejector pump problems tend to start small. Catch them before the basin overflows:

tiles.body: A sealed basin shouldn't smell. An odor points to a failed seal, a vent problem or a basin that isn't emptying.

tiles.h3: Basement Fixtures Draining Slowly or Backing Up
tiles.body: If the basement toilet, shower or laundry backs up while upstairs drains work fine, the ejector pump is the first suspect.
Many basins have a high-water alarm. If it's sounding, stop using basement fixtures and call.
A pump that runs nonstop or grinds is working against a stuck float, a failed check valve or a worn motor.

blocks.h2: Ejector Pumps in Highland Park Homes
blocks.intro: Ejector pumps show up wherever a home has plumbing below the main sewer line, like a basement bathroom, laundry or wet bar.

items.body: Nearly half of Highland Park homes were built before 1960. If a basement bathroom or laundry was added in a later remodel, it likely relies on an ejector pump that may now be reaching its age.

items.h3: Part of Every Overhead Sewer System
items.body: An [overhead sewer system](/highland-park/overhead-sewer-systems) reroutes basement drains into a pit, and an ejector pump lifts that wastewater above flood level. If you have an overhead system, your ejector pump is what keeps it working.

blocks.h2: What Happens When You Call J. Blanton
blocks.intro: An ejector pump failure is a sewage problem, so we treat it like one.

steps.body: Our phone line is open nights, weekends and holidays. Stop using basement fixtures and call.
A stuck float or a failed check valve is a repair. A burned-out motor in an older pump is a replacement. We'll tell you which one you need.
You get a flat rate before any work begins.

blocks.h2: Ejector Pump Questions From Highland Park Homeowners

items.q: What's the difference between an ejector pump and a sump pump?
items.preview: A sump pump removes groundwater. An ejector pump moves wastewater from basement fixtures to the sewer.
items.answer: A sump pump removes groundwater from a pit and pumps it outside. An ejector pump moves wastewater from basement fixtures, like a toilet or laundry, up to the main sewer line. They look similar but they're not interchangeable.

items.q: How long does an ejector pump last?
items.preview: Often 7 to 10 years or more, depending on use. Older or noisy pumps are worth checking.
items.answer: Many ejector pumps last somewhere between 7 and 10 years or more, depending on use and what goes down the basement drains. If yours is older, noisy or running more than it used to, it's worth having it checked before it fails.

items.q: What should I do if my ejector pump alarm goes off?
items.preview: Stop using basement fixtures, don't open the basin, and call us.
items.answer: Stop using every fixture that drains to the basin: basement toilet, shower, sink and washer. Don't open the sealed basin. Then call us. We'll find out why the pump isn't keeping up and fix it.

items.q: How much does ejector pump replacement cost?
items.preview: It depends on the pump, basin and access. You get a flat price before we start.
items.answer: It depends on the pump, the basin, the check valve and venting, and how easy the basin is to reach. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
